prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "MORGAN STANLEY" (ticker MS), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MS", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Morgan Stanley
result.industry: Investment banking, trading and wealth management
markets: Wealth management and brokerage (Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, E*TRADE, Morgan Stanley at Work)
Equity sales and trading, prime brokerage and financing
Investment banking (M&A advisory, equity and debt underwriting)
Asset management (Morgan Stanley Investment Management, Eaton Vance, Parametric)
Lending to wealth and corporate clients

mission.statement: Morgan Stanley helps people, institutions and governments raise, manage and distribute the capital they need to achieve their goals.
mission.source: Morgan Stanley company website (About Us / core values page); the firm also says that since 1935 it has delivered "first-class business in a first-class way"
mission.plain: Morgan Stanley helps people, companies and governments raise, invest and look after money so they can reach their goals.

about.plain: Morgan Stanley is a big Wall Street firm. It helps large companies sell shares and bonds, buy other companies, and trade stocks and bonds. It also looks after the savings and investments of millions of families through financial advisors and the E*TRADE app. And it runs investment funds for pension plans and other big savers.
about.customers: Wealthy families and everyday investors, employees who get company stock, big companies, governments, pension funds and hedge funds.
about.everyday: Many people buy stocks on the E*TRADE app or get their employer's stock-plan shares through Morgan Stanley at Work, both owned by Morgan Stanley.

money.plain: (share of 2025 net revenues of $70,645M) trading stocks and bonds for big investors, advising on mergers, raising money for companies
financial advisors, E*TRADE brokerage, workplace stock plans and loans for savers
investment funds and custom index portfolios (Parametric) for institutions and individuals
spot crypto trading on E*TRADE (pilot from May 2026) and the Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust (MSBT) launched in 2026

result.summary: Morgan Stanley has a real but moderate-to-strong moat: a top-two global equities franchise, an elite investment-banking brand, and above all a wealth and asset management business with $10.5 trillion of client assets (Q3 2026) whose sticky, fee-based relationships produced $356.3B of net new assets in 2025. Scale in wealth management, the switching costs of advisor relationships and workplace plans, and its brand give it 20%+ returns on tangible equity, but trading and banking remain cyclical and fiercely contested.

pricingPower.evidence: Advisor-led wealth management still charges asset-based fees on $3,155B of fee-based client assets (Q3 2026) while fee-based flows doubled to $80.5B in the quarter, and the E*TRADE crypto pilot charges 50 basis points per trade; but trading spreads, underwriting fees and online brokerage commissions are set by intense competition (online stock commissions are zero).

moats.evidence: Founded in 1935, Morgan Stanley is one of the two elite US investment-bank brands with Goldman Sachs, a name that wins mandates in IPOs, M&A and with wealthy clients.

Wealth clients with a financial advisor, lending, cash management and tax-managed portfolios rarely move, and companies using Morgan Stanley at Work stock-plan administration feed employees into the firm; Wealth Management pre-tax margin reached 30.4% in Q3 2026.
Its equities and prime brokerage franchise benefits from liquidity: more client flow improves pricing and financing, helping equity net revenues reach $5,799M in Q3 2026, up 41% year on year.

With $10.5 trillion of client assets, $2,046B of Investment Management AUM and $70.6B of 2025 net revenues it spreads technology, compliance and research costs over one of the largest bases in the industry.
Global trading and investment banking at bulge-bracket scale is limited to a handful of firms with the capital, licences and global reach to serve the largest clients.
Its 2009-2021 pivot to wealth (Smith Barney, E*TRADE in 2020, Eaton Vance in 2021) was a strategic shift, but rivals such as Goldman Sachs and UBS can and do pursue the same model.
Decades of risk management, prime brokerage and derivatives know-how, plus its integrated advisor-plus-digital-plus-workplace funnel, are hard to replicate quickly.
A large force of experienced financial advisors and senior bankers, and a strategic alliance with Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group in Japan, are assets few rivals can match.

customers.evidence: Wealth Management gathered $356.3B of net new assets in 2025 (up from $251.7B in 2024) and $232.4B in Q3 2026 alone, showing strong client loyalty and attraction of new money.

talent.evidence: With about 83,000 employees in 42 countries, it is a top destination for finance graduates; 93% of employees said they were proud to work there in its 2025 survey and voluntary attrition was 9%.

product.evidence: It is a global leader in equities trading (best equity topline of the big banks in Q3 2025 per Global Trading) and a top-tier M&A and IPO adviser, and its wealth platform combines advisors, E*TRADE and workplace plans in one ecosystem.

threats: A downturn in markets would cut trading, underwriting and asset-based wealth fees at the same time (net revenues fell from $59,755M in 2021 to $53,668M in 2022)
Equity trading strength ($5,799M in Q3 2026, up 41%) may not last, while investment banking fees slightly missed expectations in Q3 2026
Low-cost platforms (Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood) and independent advisor networks (LPL, Raymond James) pressure advisory fees and recruit advisors
Regulatory and anti-money-laundering scrutiny of wealth management, plus capital rules for large banks
Private-credit funds and electronic market makers such as Citadel Securities taking share of lending and trading
Credit losses on corporate and commercial real-estate loans ($105M of Institutional Securities charge-offs in Q3 2026)

ceo.name: Ted Pick
ceo.background: Joined Morgan Stanley in 1990 and rose through equities to lead Institutional Securities; Harvard BA, Stanford MBA; CEO since January 2024 and chairman since 2025

c1.evidence: Morgan Stanley is a leader in equities trading and wealth management, but these are mature, cyclical industries rather than emerging fast-growth ones.

c2.evidence: Clients choose it for its elite brand, top-tier equities and advisory franchise and advisor-led wealth platform ($356.3B of net new assets in 2025), advantages built over decades, but Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and UBS offer similar services.

c3.evidence: The name is widely known and E*TRADE is a household brand, but it is not the single default leader the way Google or NVIDIA are; JPMorgan is generally seen as the top bank.

c4.evidence: Its stated purpose to help people and institutions "raise, manage and distribute the capital they need" and its "first-class business in a first-class way" motto are long-standing, but the firm is run mainly for returns (ROTCE target of 20%+).

c6.evidence: “Wall Street, elite, wealthy, powerful” - the impression is respect for its prestige and competence, mixed with general distrust of big Wall Street banks; mostly neutral to positive.

c7.evidence: Global wealth and capital markets are huge and growing with asset values and the generational wealth transfer, but this rides markets and GDP rather than a fast secular trend like AI.

c8.evidence: It is pushing into crypto (spot trading on E*TRADE for 8.6 million clients and its MSBT bitcoin ETF in 2026), workplace wealth and private markets, but these are extensions of its existing businesses.

m1.evidence: Ted Pick talks of an 'integrated firm' targeting $10 trillion-plus of client assets (reached $10.5 trillion in Q3 2026), a clear but incremental vision continuing James Gorman's strategy.

m2.evidence: Pick is not a founder but a 36-year Morgan Stanley lifer who joined in 1990 and has spent his whole career building the firm.

m4.evidence: He emphasises client service and a 'culture of rigor, humility and partnership', but also cut about 2% of the workforce in March 2026.

m5.evidence: Morgan Stanley has a strong partnership culture and was an early adopter of generative AI tools for advisors (with OpenAI), but it is not known as a product inventor.

m6.evidence: Pick is deeply hands-on with markets and trading, having run equities and Institutional Securities, but has a history and business background rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: He has a reputation for integrity and the firm stresses giving back, but there is no evidence of a mission bigger than serving clients and shareholders well.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Ted Pick giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Pick is a low-key, measured executive rather than a famous public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2024, net revenues rose from $54,143M (2023) to $70,645M (2025) and diluted EPS from $5.18 to $10.21, with Q3 2026 ROTCE of 22.6%.

m10.evidence: Morgan Stanley is not known for frugality; compensation and benefits were $29,216M in 2025 and its efficiency ratio is about 67-68%.

c10.evidence: It helps millions of savers invest and helps companies and governments raise capital worldwide, but its impact is indirect rather than life-changing for billions.

p2.evidence: Running a global trading and risk business with $1.68 trillion of assets is very hard and capital markets matter to the economy, but the services are offered by several rivals.

f2.evidence: Pre-tax margin was 29.6% in 2020, 32.9% in 2021, 26.3% in 2022, 21.8% in 2023 and 31.1% in 2025, volatile rather than steadily rising (banks report no gross margin).

f3.evidence: Like all large dealers it is highly leveraged: $392,556M of borrowings versus $160,135M of cash at June 30, 2026, though common equity is positive at $106,579M and CET1 is 14.9%.

f4.evidence: Pre-tax income rose from $14,418M (2020) to $21,954M (2025) but dipped to $11,813M in 2023, and bank operating cash flow swings with trading balances.

v1.evidence: It is among the best in equities trading and advisor-led wealth management, but there is no single clear reason for an ordinary person to pick it over Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan or Merrill.

v2.evidence: It is a sought-after employer in finance (93% of employees proud to work there in 2025), but it does not appear near the top of broad best-place-to-work rankings and hours are long.

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, its wealth clients, E*TRADE users and corporate clients would notice the disruption, but rivals would quickly absorb most of its business.
